text.p: Swiss-French temporary employment firm Adecco said on Thursday its 1997 first-half results were up strongly and it remained optimistic for the rest of the year.
"We hope for an even better performance in the seasonally stronger second half," said John Bowmer, president of Adecco's management board in a statement released with half-year results.
Analysts were mixed in their assessment. Some were waiting for the outcome of an analysts' telephone conference this evening.

Adecco, formed last year by merging Swiss Adia and France's Ecco, said net profits before goodwill amortisation rose 36 percent to 129.2 million Swiss francs ($85.4 million) in the 1997 first half from 95.2 million in the 1996 first half, on a proforma basis.
Revenues were reported up 29 percent in the first half at 5.06 billion Swiss francs from a pro forma 3.93 billion.
"I would say that revenue growth was stronger than I expected, especially outside of France, and in North America," said Credit Suisse First Boston analyst Christoph Gretler.
But, at the same time he said news Adecco's operating margin in the reporting period fell to 4.0 percent from 4.2 percent was slightly disappointing.

Adecco, reporting its first half results, said the drop in the operating margin "reflects price pressure in certain countries, as well as higher costs in connection with the opening of new offices, and also the worldwide launch of the Adecco name."

Gretler had rated Adecco "hold" in a report published July 23. He still considered it a hold, but was waiting to hear what management said regarding the operating margin and the prospect for the next two quarters.
Frederick Hasslauer, analyst at Bank Sal. Oppenheim Jr & Cie, rated Adecco a long-term buy.

He estimated Adecco's growth in the first half in France at roughly 15 percent once currency factors were taken into account, which was about half the rate of growth France of Adecco's rival in size, U.S. firm Manpower Inc.
But Adecco was already well-represented in France.

Both the world's two largest temping firms, Adecco and Manpower, were gaining market share in France, and that was positive, he said: "If the underlying (French) market is growing at seven or eight percent, the smaller players are losing market share."
He believed prospects for Adecco were better overall.
He favoured Adecco over Manpower partly because of its strong presence in Europe, and also due to its sensitivity to the U.S. dollar, which has lately appreciated against European currencies.

Adecco's North American growth was driven in particular by demand for specialist services. Adecco reported what Hasslauer called a "huge leap" in its revenues for special brands, rising in first half 1997 by 79 percent, to 496 million Swiss francs from 277 million.
The special brands business was being driven by demand for white collar temps, "and it is there that Adecco is particularly strong," Hasslauer said.
He also expected it to make an aquisition in North America.

At the same time, he believed temporary employment firms would make further inroads in Europe, including in Italy after recent liberalisation there. He said that there was also a strong U.S. multinational presence in Italy which should help demand in the wake of recent liberalisations. The Spanish market was also growing, he said.
"The temp market continues to penetrate (into) Europe," he said.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340 ($ = 1.513 Swiss Francs)
